notable_claims: Computer administrators lacked the tradition of demanding subpoenas and warrants that librarians possessed.
The University of Western Ontario did not guarantee protection for users against police action.
classification.summary: This item discusses the legal and ethical tensions regarding university computer administrators' cooperation with police in the 'Homolka FAQ' case. It highlights a contrast between the established privacy traditions of librarians and the lack of similar protections or training among network security officers.

notable_claims: University computer administrators lacked the tradition of demanding warrants that librarians possessed.
Law enforcement agencies were confused about whether possessing a digital file constituted a breach of a publication ban.
The Internet allows users to circumvent traditional censorious power structures.
classification.summary: An article from Toronto's 'eye' magazine details how police and university administrators targeted students for distributing a forbidden FAQ about the Karla Homolka trial. It highlights a case where University of Western Ontario staff froze a student's account and cooperated with police without a warrant. The piece emphasizes the lack of professional ethics among early computer administrators compared to librarians regarding user privacy.
classification.title: Policing the New Media -- Internet users have their liberty threatened as law enforcement agencies blunder about trying (and failing) to enforce the Homolka press ban

notable_claims: Monash University banned alt.sex.* newsgroups to prevent sexual harassment via public terminals.
classification.summary: Monash University, acting as a major news gateway in Australia, banned all sex-related newsgroups to prevent students from displaying pornographic images on public terminals. The ban initially included the alt.sexual.abuse.recovery group, though it was later restored following a specific request. This incident highlights early institutional struggles with balancing network access and acceptable use policies.
classification.title: Monash University censoring alt.sex.*

notable_claims: Monash University implemented a policy to block newsgroups matching alt.sex* and alt.binaries.pictures.erotica* based on sexual harassment policies.
classification.summary: A user reports that Monash University, acting as a major news gateway in Australia, was filtering Usenet groups matching 'alt.sex*' and 'alt.binaries.pictures.erotica*' to prevent sexual harassment and pornography. The user successfully requested an exception for the ASAR (Academic System Administrators Research) group by refining the filter pattern. This highlights early institutional efforts to regulate content on academic networks.
classification.title: Monash University censoring alt.sex.*

notable_claims: Speech codes adopted by government-financed state colleges amount to government censorship.
The ACLU successfully challenged speech codes at the Universities of Connecticut, Michigan, and Wisconsin.
Defending free speech for bigots is necessary to protect the rights of civil rights activists.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares an ACLU briefing paper arguing that campus speech codes prohibiting offensive language violate the First Amendment and undermine academic freedom. The document asserts that 'more speech' is the appropriate remedy for bigotry and warns that such codes are often used against the very minority groups they intend to protect.
classification.title: [ACLU] "Hate Speech On Campus"

notable_claims: Restricting computer systems to specific academic purposes is an allocation of scarce resources, not censorship.
System administrators have an obligation to identify users for the police when requested, especially if the identity is already known.
classification.summary: Reg Quinton, a university computer security officer at Western (UWO), defends the restriction of computer systems to specific academic purposes and the disclosure of user identity to police. He argues that limiting system use to instructional goals is an allocation of scarce resources rather than censorship. The discussion centers on the balance between user rights, administrative obligations, and legal compliance in a university setting.

classification.summary: A report describes a student at Warwick University who lost computer system access after posting satirical content to soc.culture.columbia. The student was reportedly expelled from the system again after posting a critique of the system administrator's fairness.

notable_claims: A university system administrator suspended a student's account for newsgroup postings without specifying which rules were broken.
The student felt compelled to apologize to regain network access due to upcoming exams.
classification.summary: A student at the University of Warwick describes being suspended from their network account by a system administrator for making 'inappropriate' postings to a newsgroup. The student reports that university staff dismissed free speech concerns, stating 'this is not America,' and notes they were forced to apologize to regain access before exams. A subsequent post discussing the incident led to a second account suspension.
classification.title: Re: Net Censorship Case!!!
